COVID: FUTURE OF RESTAURANTS

By: Nicky Troll | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
If the restaurant industry is to survive in a world reshaped by COVID-19, restaurants will have to re-invent themselves - we look at the status quo, the future and the rise of dark kitchens.

Summary:
Many restaurants face a difficult trade-off: while deliveries will bring in some income, it may not be enough to cover operating costs of re-opening bigger establishments.

But at this stage it’s a matter of liquidation or take-aways for most restaurant owners in South Africa.

Are restaurant experiences a thing of the past? What will it take to come out standing without crumbing under the pressure of an economy crippled by COVID-19?

Further information:
RENTAL ROULETTE
While the Property Industry Group – which represents SA’s largest mall owners – announced that restaurants won’t have to pay any rent in April, with discounts of 55% in May and 45% in June – smaller restaurants in standalone set ups are feeling the heat and many will be forced to get out of the kitchen.

Some franchise restaurants are opting not to open under LockDown Level 4 – they say with the social distancing restrictions they’re businesses ran at huge losses in the weeks leading up to Level 5 LockDown – these include Spur, Ocean Basket, Nandos, KFC.

In the run-up to lockdown in March, restaurants weren’t allowed to sell alcohol after 18:00, and were restricted to a maximum of 50 people (including staff).

In a letter to its landlords, Spur group's chief operating officer Mark Farrelly said that it would be “commercial suicide” to reopen under those conditions.

Nandos are not re-opening for the public – they’ve opted to open a few store to cook for the poor. I think they’re a better bet than Spur (can’t reach them at this stage). The Nandos franchise story is a great South Africa success story – having started in SA and closed during apartheid unrest – they’ll work well on camera.

DELIVERY OR DON’T EVEN DARE
The cost of delivery is also high: for example, Uber Eats asks outlets up to 30% commission on each meal ordered on its platform. Mr D – takes 25% of the meal price. And as restaurants start to earn money, their landlords are expected to take a tougher line in claiming rent.

INDEPENDENT RESTAURANTS
Small businesses are bearing the biggest brunt with ruthless landlords – the restaurant industry doesn’t allow for business to make double the turn over when they get to trade – the lockdown month is lost forever for many of these businesses.

It also changes the way restaurants will operate in the future as Retail Futurist Howard Saunders explains:
Very soon we will understand that retail and hospitality were never really about buying more stuff or filling our bellies. Our industry is all about human engagement and post-C19 I expect shops and restaurants to welcome us more warmly and sincerely than at any time since the festive period.

Sadly, as C19 proliferates, we are unlikely to be dancing and hugging in the streets as in 1945. Masks and visors will become standard dress, and restaurant staff will be obliged to wear protective gear for insurance purposes. Tables will be widely spaced and prices will have to rise accordingly. But with unemployment at 30% very few will be able to afford the luxury of dining out, so it will feel like a return to the 1960s.

CASE STUDY
Sean & Marcelle Roberts own an iconic Durban fine dining restaurant – Café ’99, as well as a bar and brewery. They have never done take aways – they offers patrons dining experiences – but with rentals due, bills piling up the couple have been forced to reinvent their business model – switching to takeaways for the first time in 20 years.

It’s a lovely example of the challenges faced by smaller operators who are working from independent sights outside of big malls and big franchises.

DARK KITCHENS
Is this possibly the rise of Dark Kitchens – replacing the restaurant experienced with a sanitised delivery only service to titilate tastebuds. It’s a concept where food is prepared at takeaway premises rather than a restaurant. Compared to a usual takeaway format, however, orders are placed online, without the option for the public to enter the premises.

Heini Booysen has started a chain of “hidden” or “ghost” restaurants in Cape Town – Darth Kitchen – they run a dark kitchen for 5 restaurants for delivery only. He was also one of the founders of Orderin and has first hand knowledge and experience of the delivery industry – so he can speak to the business models and economic challenges faced by both restaurants and delivery services.

RESTAURANT ASSOCIATION OF SA
They represent over 1000 restaurants and over 60 000 employees - they will give an industry perspective. CEO Wendy Alberts feels the way of the future will one where experience dining is a thing of the past, but where restaurants will have to try to cut costs and provide affordable accessible meals to the masses. (nice tie in to Nandos feeding angle)

* DARTH KITCHENS IS IN CAPE TOWN
* CAFE '99 IS IN DURBAN

Press Release:


The Future of Restaurants
What will the restaurant of the future look like or has a romantic evening of fine dining been completely relegated to the past? Restricted from selling alcohol for consumption on site and forced to implement delivery and collection services for all meal purchases, the impact of the ongoing national lockdown has turned business upside down for the restaurant industry. Some waitrons have had to adapt and become delivery drivers while traditional sit-in establishments now also provide drive-thru services for their patrons. Carte Blanche explores how these businesses are re-inventing themselves in a bid to survive in a world that’s been reshaped by the COVID-19 pandemic.
Producer: Nicky Troll | Presenter: Masa Kekana


Script:


STRUCTURE

VO: In world dramatically reshaped by COIVD-19, the days of dining out in a restaurant are long gone.

Social distancing and lockdown regulations have forced restaurants to close, stack up tables and chairs and turn off the stoves.

LINK: NOT BEING ABLE TO TRADE HAS HAD DIRE CONSEQUENCES FOR THE RESTAURANT INDUSTRY AROUND THE WORLD, SOUTH AFRICA HAS NOT BEEN IMMUNE – COULD THIS BE THE END OF RESTAURANTS AS WE KNOW IT?

HOWARD: it is a cull. Some won't survive. It's not pretty and it's going to be very painful for many

VO: A harsh reality for many local restaurateurs. Durban Chef Marcelle Roberts owns a fine dining restaurant, a bar and a brewery.

All three establishments immediately felt the heat when COVID-19 hit South Africa in March.

MARCELLE: We saw our turnover dropping daily. The trouble started when the alcohol sales were banned after 6:00 p.m. It felt surreal… it just started snowballing.

VO: International Chef and Johannesburg Restaurant owner Wandile Mabaso, says the losses during Lockdown Level 5 were crippling.

WANDILE: During the 36 days of lockdown itself we probably lost about one point five million. This is in money.

VO: As fear mounted, business grinded to a halt and Wandile decided to close even before Level 5 was officially implemented.

WANDILE: It does not make financial sense to have all of the staff, all of the labour, the lights the energy and everything out there with no customers coming in.

VO: It’s an industry on its knees explains Wendy Alberts from the Restaurant Association of South Africa.

WENDY: With limited turnover there's no ways we can afford the exponential cost to run a restaurant. The margins are just simply too small. So the debt is just escalating and it's just compounding and all the relief that there has been for the few restaurants that have obtained it is further loans.

MARCELLE: It all depends on the rental breaks that we are going to get from our landlords from you know bank charges. Point of Sale rentals that we still have to pay. We can't carry on paying that for much longer if we can't trade. None of us want to admit that we wanna close our doors.

VO: The industry was thrown a lifeline with take-aways for delivery only permitted under Level Four Lockdown.

LINK: UNDER THE NEW REGULATIONS, MANY ESTABLISHMENTS ARE ADAPTING THEIR BUSINESS MODELS IN A DESPERATE ATTEMPT TO SURVIVE – FOR MANY IT’S A CASE OF DO TAKEAWAYS OR LIQUIDATE // [OR GO BROKE]

WANDILE: It's difficult to deliver fine dining food because it's delicate and it's the ingredients are always good quality ingredients and usually expensive. So it changed our whole business. Now we have to prepare ourselves for food deliveries. That itself is a problem because we don't even make about 50 percent of our usual revenue from deliveries.

VO: Some of the major franchise chains like Spur and Ocean Basket have opted not open under these regulations – saying it’s just not economically viable to just to deliveries.

WENDY: you look at the prospective potential of turnover you're looking at round about 20 percent of a hundred percent of turnover.

VO: Marcelle’s food experience restaurants were not set up for the take-away market – but they’ve jumped at the chance to start trading again and have opened one restaurant for deliveries while also taking up an opportunity to produce frozen meals.

MARCELLE: yad yada……. Think outside of the box

LINK: COVID-19 HAS CHALLENGED HOW WE DO ABSOLUTELY EVERYTHING, HOW WE WORK, HOW WE INTERACT AND HOW WE TRAVEL – IT WILL ALSO CHANGE HOW WE ENJOY FOOD AND DINING-OUT EXPERIENCES.

WENDY: we have to look at mechanisms both from an economical point of view and a social point of view that brings trust and brings comfort and brings confidence in the consumer that restaurants are a place that you can enjoy a meal that is that you know more dressed and going to grab your shopping basket at a supermarket

VO: UK based Retail Futurist Howard Saunders, believes traditional restaurants will be transformed to deal with safety conscious consumers.

HOWARD: The tables will be more widely spaced. Some of the restaurants will have to put their prices up accordingly because they're serving fewer Customers. There'll be mask wearing servers.

VO: In Amsterdam, an innovative restaurant has built Quarantine Greenhouses – offering customers the pleasure of dining out and the assurance that they are safe.

Alberts believes we could see the return old style road house operations.

WENDY: A part of it again where people can enjoy a meal in their car car parks will be able to become an extension of the restaurants. You know if we look at what opportunities they are futuristic or restaurants in so many probabilities in terms of contactless engagements and connections.

VO: But it’s human connections that people will crave most in the future reckons Saunders.

HOWARD: Hospitality is a social lubricant. It's how we meet people it's how we fall in love it's how we make business deals. // without hospitality with become kind of a //soulless Planet

VO: In South Africa though, Level Four Regulations lends itself to the rise of Dark Kitchens – a global trend that’s seems to be a financially viable option for restaurants in these times.

Tom Shackle runs four independent brands from one kitchen in Cape Town – saving costs on working space and staff.

TOM: WE only deliver food. We've got no customer facing operation we've got no tables and chairs no waiters. instead of only having one cuisine type one brand coming out of a kitchen. We can actually operate multiple brands coming out of one operation
VO: While the rise of dark kitchens is inevitable in a post-COVID world, it does not necessarily mean the demise of traditional restaurants according to Saunders.

HOWARD: the truth is we don't really go to restaurants and bars because we need to drink or we're hungry - we're going to want to connect with humans even more so. We've been kept away from it. We've been we've been starved of real hospitality. We're going to want that back.

VO: But getting back to business as usual pre-COVID won’t be quick and it will demand change.

Wandile does comprehensive screening and constant sanitizing is mandatory. He’s also divided the reduced staff into two teams to avoid a complete shut down should an infection be confirmed.

But doing the right thing is not cheap.

WANDILE: // we've just had to learn that this is very expensive sanitizer is expensive. You know if we are saying that people must wash their hands which we are saying in our kitchen every five minutes so you can imagine how much soap is costing us a week.

VO: Wandile’s also set up his own delivery service, using waiting staff as packers and runners – limiting potential contact.

WANDILE: We did not opt to go to the mainstream delivery services because they take a huge percentage - And at this time we don't need anybody taking anything from us.

VO: While third party delivery services have been widely criticised for their fee structure, Tom explains it’s tough balancing back.

TOM: These guys need to make money…// Fortunately we've been able to model our business and model all of our different brands around factoring in that 20 to 30 percent commission. But for other restaurants who are now operating solely off delivery platform across the country it's very, very difficult for them to suddenly have to factor in that commission on what was only maybe a percentage of their turnover previously.

VO: Alberts says it’s time for Government to step up - the current regulations are simply too stringent, she argues there’s a strong case for customers to collect their own orders.

WENDY: A typical delivery person can have 20 to 30 points of contact depending on how many deliveries they have done, where a consumer that leaves home and collects their meal from curb-side collection. That's pretty much contactless. So there's no point of contact other than the preparation of the meal.

VO: With the industry operating at restricted capacity, many restaurants are also struggling to meet rental obligations.

While Restaurants in some of the bigger malls got rent free for April and discounts in May and June – smaller restaurants outside of malls maybe forced out of the kitchen.

WENDY: The landlords are expecting us to go back to these really big leases and really large rentals which we just can't simply do. There's been restriction after restriction difficulty after difficulty.

VO: Saunders explains that even landlords will be subjected to change in a post-COVID world and will need to accept lower rentals – the playing field has essentially been levelled.

HOWARD: that allows small independents to come through to start up businesses and concept - and it will be innovative new businesses that push through

VO: But for now, local restaurateurs are just trying to make ends meet and get through COVID-19.

WANDILE: If you don't do that you will fall and you won't come back. The idea is to slowly get into the new system and accept it.

MARCELLE: we are we small businesses we do it for the love of it. We will be back - But it's going to take us very very very long to get back onto our feet.

PROMOS

PROMO 1
VO: The days of dinning out are long gone, the restaurant industry will have to be reinvented in a world reshaped by COVID-19 - we look at the status quo and future trends.

PROMO 2
VO: What will it take for the restaurant industry is to survive in a world reshaped by COVID-19? We look at the future of restaurants and ask if it’s a case of adapt or die?

PROMO 3
VO: The deadly coronavirus has left hundreds of restaurants across South Africa on their knees – is this end of an industry as we know it or can it be reinvented and survive?

It's how we meet people it's how we fall in love it's how we make business deals. // without hospitality with become kind of a //soulless Planet VO: In South Africa though, Level Four Regulations lends itself to the rise of Dark Kitchens – a global trend that’s seems to be a financially viable option for restaurants in these times. Tom Shackle runs four independent brands from one kitchen in Cape Town – saving costs on working space and staff. TOM: WE only deliver food. We've got no customer facing operation we've got no tables and chairs no waiters. instead of only having one cuisine type one brand coming out of a kitchen. We can actually operate multiple brands coming out of one operation VO: While the rise of dark kitchens is inevitable in a post-COVID world, it does not necessarily mean the demise of traditional restaurants according to Saunders. HOWARD: the truth is we don't really go to restaurants and bars because we need to drink or we're hungry - we're going to want to connect with humans even more so. We've been kept away from it. We've been we've been starved of real hospitality. We're going to want that back. VO: But getting back to business as usual pre-COVID won’t be quick and it will demand change. Wandile does comprehensive screening and constant sanitizing is mandatory. He’s also divided the reduced staff into two teams to avoid a complete shut down should an infection be confirmed. But doing the right thing is not cheap. WANDILE: // we've just had to learn that this is very expensive sanitizer is expensive. You know if we are saying that people must wash their hands which we are saying in our kitchen every five minutes so you can imagine how much soap is costing us a week. VO: Wandile’s also set up his own delivery service, using waiting staff as packers and runners – limiting potential contact. WANDILE: We did not opt to go to the mainstream delivery services because they take a huge percentage - And at this time we don't need anybody taking anything from us. VO: While third party delivery services have been widely criticised for their fee structure, Tom explains it’s tough balancing back. TOM: These guys need to make money…// Fortunately we've been able to model our business and model all of our different brands around factoring in that 20 to 30 percent commission. But for other restaurants who are now operating solely off delivery platform across the country it's very, very difficult for them to suddenly have to factor in that commission on what was only maybe a percentage of their turnover previously. VO: Alberts says it’s time for Government to step up - the current regulations are simply too stringent, she argues there’s a strong case for customers to collect their own orders. WENDY: A typical delivery person can have 20 to 30 points of contact depending on how many deliveries they have done, where a consumer that leaves home and collects their meal from curb-side collection. That's pretty much contactless. So there's no point of contact other than the preparation of the meal. VO: With the industry operating at restricted capacity, many restaurants are also struggling to meet rental obligations. While Restaurants in some of the bigger malls got rent free for April and discounts in May and June – smaller restaurants outside of malls maybe forced out of the kitchen. WENDY: The landlords are expecting us to go back to these really big leases and really large rentals which we just can't simply do. There's been restriction after restriction difficulty after difficulty. VO: Saunders explains that even landlords will be subjected to change in a post-COVID world and will need to accept lower rentals – the playing field has essentially been levelled. HOWARD: that allows small independents to come through to start up businesses and concept - and it will be innovative new businesses that push through VO: But for now, local restaurateurs are just trying to make ends meet and get through COVID-19. WANDILE: If you don't do that you will fall and you won't come back. The idea is to slowly get into the new system and accept it. MARCELLE: we are we small businesses we do it for the love of it. We will be back - But it's going to take us very very very long to get back onto our feet. PROMOS PROMO 1 VO: The days of dinning out are long gone, the restaurant industry will have to be reinvented in a world reshaped by COVID-19 - we look at the status quo and future trends. PROMO 2 VO: What will it take for the restaurant industry is to survive in a world reshaped by COVID-19? We look at the future of restaurants and ask if it’s a case of adapt or die? PROMO 3 VO: The deadly coronavirus has left hundreds of restaurants across South Africa on their knees – is this end of an industry as we know it or can it be reinvented and survive?

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): If the restaurant industry is to survive in a world reshaped by COVID-19, restaurants will have to re-invent themselves - we look at the status quo, the future and the rise of dark kitchens.
metadata.Summary: Many restaurants face a difficult trade-off: while deliveries will bring in some income, it may not be enough to cover operating costs of re-opening bigger establishments. But at this stage it’s a matter of liquidation or take-aways for most restaurant owners in South Africa. Are restaurant experiences a thing of the past? What will it take to come out standing without crumbing under the pressure of an economy crippled by COVID-19?
metadata.Further information: RENTAL ROULETTE While the Property Industry Group – which represents SA’s largest mall owners – announced that restaurants won’t have to pay any rent in April, with discounts of 55% in May and 45% in June – smaller restaurants in standalone set ups are feeling the heat and many will be forced to get out of the kitchen. Some franchise restaurants are opting not to open under LockDown Level 4 – they say with the social distancing restrictions they’re businesses ran at huge losses in the weeks leading up to Level 5 LockDown – these include Spur, Ocean Basket, Nandos, KFC. In the run-up to lockdown in March, restaurants weren’t allowed to sell alcohol after 18:00, and were restricted to a maximum of 50 people (including staff). In a letter to its landlords, Spur group's chief operating officer Mark Farrelly said that it would be “commercial suicide” to reopen under those conditions. Nandos are not re-opening for the public – they’ve opted to open a few store to cook for the poor. I think they’re a better bet than Spur (can’t reach them at this stage). The Nandos franchise story is a great South Africa success story – having started in SA and closed during apartheid unrest – they’ll work well on camera. DELIVERY OR DON’T EVEN DARE The cost of delivery is also high: for example, Uber Eats asks outlets up to 30% commission on each meal ordered on its platform. Mr D – takes 25% of the meal price. And as restaurants start to earn money, their landlords are expected to take a tougher line in claiming rent. INDEPENDENT RESTAURANTS Small businesses are bearing the biggest brunt with ruthless landlords – the restaurant industry doesn’t allow for business to make double the turn over when they get to trade – the lockdown month is lost forever for many of these businesses. It also changes the way restaurants will operate in the future as Retail Futurist Howard Saunders explains: Very soon we will understand that retail and hospitality were never really about buying more stuff or filling our bellies. Our industry is all about human engagement and post-C19 I expect shops and restaurants to welcome us more warmly and sincerely than at any time since the festive period. Sadly, as C19 proliferates, we are unlikely to be dancing and hugging in the streets as in 1945. Masks and visors will become standard dress, and restaurant staff will be obliged to wear protective gear for insurance purposes. Tables will be widely spaced and prices will have to rise accordingly. But with unemployment at 30% very few will be able to afford the luxury of dining out, so it will feel like a return to the 1960s. CASE STUDY Sean & Marcelle Roberts own an iconic Durban fine dining restaurant – Café ’99, as well as a bar and brewery. They have never done take aways – they offers patrons dining experiences – but with rentals due, bills piling up the couple have been forced to reinvent their business model – switching to takeaways for the first time in 20 years. It’s a lovely example of the challenges faced by smaller operators who are working from independent sights outside of big malls and big franchises. DARK KITCHENS Is this possibly the rise of Dark Kitchens – replacing the restaurant experienced with a sanitised delivery only service to titilate tastebuds. It’s a concept where food is prepared at takeaway premises rather than a restaurant. Compared to a usual takeaway format, however, orders are placed online, without the option for the public to enter the premises. Heini Booysen has started a chain of “hidden” or “ghost” restaurants in Cape Town – Darth Kitchen – they run a dark kitchen for 5 restaurants for delivery only. He was also one of the founders of Orderin and has first hand knowledge and experience of the delivery industry – so he can speak to the business models and economic challenges faced by both restaurants and delivery services. RESTAURANT ASSOCIATION OF SA They represent over 1000 restaurants and over 60 000 employees - they will give an industry perspective. CEO Wendy Alberts feels the way of the future will one where experience dining is a thing of the past, but where restaurants will have to try to cut costs and provide affordable accessible meals to the masses.
